summary: Defines a way for a mobile node to identify itself by including its Network Access Identifier in the Mobile IP registration request. It also updates RFC 2290 for the Mobile-IPv4 option in IPCP. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: A traveling device shows a name tag when it signs in on a new network, so the home network knows it.

questions: how does a mobile node identify itself
what is the mobile node nai extension
what is mobile ip extension type 131
what are mobile ip error codes 96 to 99
can a mobile node have a zero home address
subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IP device can sign in with a user name instead of a fixed home address.

tldr.problem: AAA servers identify dial-up clients by their Network Access Identifier (NAI), but a Mobile IP registration only identifies the mobile node by its home address, which it may not even have yet.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node adds a Mobile Node NAI extension (type 131) carrying its NAI to the Registration Request, and may set the Home Address field to zero to ask that one be assigned. Four new error codes (96 to 99) cover missing pieces.
tldr.outcome: A mobile node can be authenticated and authorized by a foreign domain with AAA servers using only its NAI. The RFC also updates RFC 2290 so the Home Address in its PPP option may be zero.

facts.label: Extension order
facts.value: Before the Mobile-Home and Mobile-Foreign Authentication extensions

today: RFC 2794 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It updates RFC 2290, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
AAA servers already provide authentication and authorization for dial-up computers, and the RFC argues they are just as useful for mobile nodes that visit foreign domains with AAA servers. Those servers identify clients by the Network Access Identifier (NAI). This document defines a Mobile Node NAI extension to the Mobile IP Registration Request defined in RFC 2002.

Because the NAI normally identifies the mobile node uniquely, the home address is not always needed to do that job. A node can therefore be authenticated and authorized without having a home address at all. A message with the extension MAY set the Home Address field to zero in the Registration Request to ask that a home address be assigned.
sections.eli5: Instead of showing a house number, the traveling device shows its name. The network can then look it up and hand it a house number to use.

sections.title: The Mobile Node NAI Extension
sections.content:
The extension holds the user name in the format defined by the NAI specification, RFC 2486. It has three fields: Type is 131 and marks the extension as skippable, Length is the length in bytes of the MN-NAI field, and MN-NAI is the NAI string itself.

When the extension is in a Registration Request, the Home Address field MAY be zero. The extension MUST appear before both the Mobile-Home Authentication extension and the Mobile-Foreign Authentication extension, if those are present.
sections.eli5: The extension is a small label with three parts: what kind of label it is, how long the name is, and the name itself. It goes before the secret-code parts of the message.

sections.title: Foreign Agent Behavior
sections.content:
If the Home Address in a Registration Request is zero, the foreign agent MUST use the NAI instead in its pending registration request records, together with the Identification field as usual. A foreign agent that cannot keep its records this way MUST return a Registration Reply with the Code NONZERO_HOMEADDR_REQD.

If the request carried the extension, the home agent's Registration Reply MUST include it too. If it does not, the foreign agent SHOULD forward the reply to the mobile node with the Code changed to MISSING_NAI. The reply MUST also carry a nonzero Home Agent address and the mobile node's Home Address. If either is missing, the foreign agent SHOULD change the Code to MISSING_HOME_AGENT or MISSING_HOMEADDR.
sections.eli5: The helper at the new network keeps track of waiting requests by name when there is no house number. If the answer comes back without the name, the home address or the home helper, the helper tells the traveler something is missing.

sections.title: Interaction with the IPCP Option
sections.content:
RFC 2290 defines the Mobile-IPv4 Configuration option for PPP's IPCP, and it said the Mobile Node's Home Address field MUST not be zero. This RFC updates that rule: when the node identifies itself by NAI and obtains an address after the PPP phase, the field MAY be zero. All other aspects of RFC 2290 are kept.

Whatever the option contains, the mobile node then tries to obtain a home address from the Mobile IP Registration Reply. For the IP Address Configuration Option in IPCP, the RFC gives three cases:

  • Address equal to zero: the PPP peer is expected to allocate and assign a co-located care-of address.
  • Nonzero address: the PPP peer is expected to assign that address as the co-located care-of address.
  • Option left out of the IPCP Configure-Request: no co-located care-of address is assigned during IPCP. The node gets one later or uses an FA-located care-of address.
sections.eli5: The older rules said the house number box on the PPP form could never be empty. Now it can be, because the traveler will get its house number later.

sections.title: New Error Codes
sections.content:
The RFC defines four Code values for Registration Replies. They sit in the range 64 to 127 that is conventionally used for rejection by the foreign agent. Section 3 above says when each is used.

The IANA is asked to assign 131 to the extension and to record the four code values.
sections.eli5: These are four error messages, each with its own number, that tell the traveler which piece of the paperwork was missing.

sections.title: Security and IPv6
sections.content:
Mobile IP registration messages are authenticated, and the recipient verifies the authentication. This proposal does not stop a mobile node from sending its NAI in the clear over the network, but the RFC does not expect that to be a security issue.

Supporting NAI-based registration for Mobile IPv6 is outside the scope of the document. It only sketches ideas: since IPv6 has no foreign agent, the NAI would have to reach a local AAA through the router or DHCPv6 server that configures the care-of address, using options that were yet to be defined.
sections.eli5: Messages are already checked to make sure they are real. Showing your name tag openly is not thought to be a problem.

sections.title: Home Domain Allocation Function
sections.content:
The appendix introduces the Home Domain Allocation Function (HDAF), which can dynamically assign a home address to a mobile node. It receives messages from foreign agents and assigns a home address within the home domain. It does no Mobile IP processing on the Registration Request; it simply forwards the request to a home agent in the network that can handle it.

The foreign agent extracts the NAI, finds the domain name in it, and then finds the HDAF for that domain. How it finds the HDAF is outside the specification. As an example, the foreign agent might delegate that to a local AAA server, which may also help verify the node's credentials using protocols not specified here.
sections.eli5: Think of a receptionist at the home office. A request comes in, the receptionist picks the right person to handle it, and passes it along without dealing with it personally.

items.label: NONZERO_HOMEADDR_REQD
items.desc: Foreign agent cannot track pending requests by NAI, so it needs a nonzero home address.

items.label: MISSING_NAI
items.desc: The reply from the home agent lacked the Mobile Node NAI extension.

items.label: MISSING_HOME_AGENT
items.desc: The reply lacked a nonzero Home Agent address.

items.label: MISSING_HOMEADDR
items.desc: The reply lacked the mobile node's Home Address.
